passage:
"I cancelled the trek," Sarika said, dropping onto the sofa. "Emailed the group."
Chinmay put down the vegetables. "The one we booked in March?"
"My body won't manage it. Not with the flare-ups." She pressed her palms to her eyes. "I'm so tired of losing things, Chinmay."
"That's a real loss. You wanted that trek for years."
"And this morning I had to take the lift at work because I couldn't face the stairs. I wanted to kick the wall."
"Fair enough."
She laughed wetly. "And then my workshop went brilliantly. Twenty people, and the director asked for my slides."
"That's huge. I'm proud of you."
"How can I be sad and angry and proud in one day?"
"Because all of it is true," Chinmay said, and sat down beside her.

qa.q: Who asked for Sarika's slides?
qa.a: The director asked for her slides.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling about the cancelled trek?
qa.a: She felt grief and weariness, tired of losing things she had wanted for years.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do that helped Sarika?
qa.a: Chinmay named her loss as real, accepted her anger without correcting it, celebrated her workshop and stayed beside her.

qa.q: What is it like for Chinmay to hear about Sarika's day?
qa.a: Chinmay seems moved and proud, sharing her sadness about the trek and her joy about the workshop without trying to fix anything.

grounding: It shows a young adult with a long-term condition feeling grief, anger and pride on the same day, with each feeling treated as valid.

passage:
Last Tuesday, I found my old dance photos while cleaning the cupboard. I sat on the floor and cried. Before my illness, I'd planned to open a studio. Now I walk with a stick on bad days.
By noon I was furious. The bus driver pulled away before I'd got both feet on the step, and I stood on the road shaking.
Then that evening I taught my Kathak class for the little ones, sitting in a chair, counting beats and correcting hands. A seven-year-old finally got her spin right and ran to hug me. I was so proud of her, and of me.
I called Pradeep and said, "Is it mad to feel all of that in one day?"
He said, "Bhai, it's not mad. It's your life. All of it counts."

Lalit

qa.q: What did Lalit find while cleaning the cupboard?
qa.a: Lalit found old dance photos.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling on the road after the bus pulled away?
qa.a: Lalit was furious and shaken, angry at being left on the road.

qa.q: Which moment of the day could Lalit hold on to, and why?
qa.a: Teaching the class and seeing the child get her spin right, because it showed that Lalit's skill and resilience still matter.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see Lalit's mixed feelings?
qa.a: Pradeep sees them as normal parts of Lalit's life, not as something mad or wrong.

grounding: It shows a person with a long-term illness feeling grief, anger and pride on one day, and a friend treating all of it as valid.

passage:
Dear Jahnavi,
You asked how I really am, so here's the honest answer.
On Monday I cried because the trek group posted photos from the pass we planned together, before my arthritis got bad. I should have been there. That still hurts.
On Wednesday I was furious because my hands wouldn't open the pickle jar, and then furious again because I needed help with my kurta buttons.
And on Friday, I walked all the way round the lake for the first time since my flare. It took me an hour and I rested on four benches. I felt so proud I nearly called you from the bench.
I used to think feeling sad meant I was being negative. Now I think grief, anger and pride can all live in one week. None of them is wrong.
Love,
Dolma

qa.q: How many benches did Dolma rest on?
qa.a: Four benches.

qa.q: What did Dolma feel on Monday?
qa.a: Dolma felt sad and hurt, grieving the trek that had been planned before the arthritis got bad.

qa.q: What does Dolma now believe about the mix of feelings?
qa.a: That grief, anger and pride can all live in one week, and none of them is wrong.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jahnavi is likely to feel moved and grateful for Dolma's honesty, and proud of the lake walk.

grounding: Shows a young adult living with a long-term condition feeling grief, frustration and pride within one week, and accepting all as valid.

passage: Reena, you asked how I'm doing with the dialysis, so let me be honest, na? It's Madhuri talking, not the brave-face Madhuri. Some mornings I wake up and grieve. I was supposed to do my master's in Germany. That plan is gone, and some days I just sit with that. Other days, I'm angry. Four hours, three times a week, hooked to a machine while everyone else goes to movies. I snapped at the nurse last week and then felt terrible. But you know what? On Tuesday I got my first salary from the online tutoring job I do from the dialysis chair. I held that message and laughed out loud. I'm proud of myself. Sad, angry and proud, sometimes before lunch. I've stopped thinking one of those is the wrong feeling.

qa.q: How often is Madhuri on dialysis?
qa.a: Four hours, three times a week.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel on getting the first salary?
qa.a: Madhuri felt proud and joyful, laughing out loud.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's story show about living with a long-term condition?
qa.a: That grief over lost plans, anger at limits and pride in resilience can all be valid, even on the same day.

qa.q: How might the nurse have felt when Madhuri snapped?
qa.a: The nurse may have felt hurt or understood that the frustration was not really about them.

grounding: Shows a young adult living with long-term illness feeling grief over lost plans, anger at limits and pride in resilience, all accepted as valid.

passage:
Monday: At his younger brother's cricket match, Anand, twenty-five, sat in his wheelchair at the boundary and felt the old grief rise. Two years ago he had captained that same team. He went quiet all evening. His partner Bidisha just held his hand.
Wednesday: The new office had a 'wheelchair entrance' that turned out to be locked. Anand waited twenty minutes in the heat, fuming, then emailed the facilities manager in sharp, clear words.
Saturday: He finished his first half-marathon in a racing chair. Bidisha screamed at the finish line. Anand laughed and cried at the same time. 'Monday, I was so low,' he said. 'Today, I'm so proud.' 'Both count,' Bidisha said.

qa.q: How long did Anand wait at the locked entrance?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Anand feel at the cricket match on Monday?
qa.a: He felt grief for the team he once captained, going quiet all evening.

qa.q: Why is Bidisha's 'Both count' a wise response?
qa.a: It accepts his grief and his pride as equally real, without calling either a bad attitude.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt at the finish line?
qa.a: She felt overjoyed and proud, screaming as he finished.

grounding: Shows a young adult living with disability feeling grief, frustration and pride within one week, all valid and none a failure of attitude.

passage: Uday, you asked how I stay so calm about my hospital mornings. I'm Alka, and I wasn't calm at twenty-five. That was the year my kidneys gave up and dialysis took three mornings of every week. I had a ticket for a trek in Ladakh that I never used. Some days I sat in the car park and cried for that trip. Some days I wanted to throw the machine out of the window because I was too tired to finish one report. And some days, sometimes the very same day, I felt proud that I'd learned the whole routine myself and still handed in my work. My mother kept telling me to "stay positive". It made me feel I was failing at feelings too. Then a nurse told me all three were allowed. That helped more than anything anyone said.

qa.q: What trip did Alka never take?
qa.a: A trek in Ladakh.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Alka have that year, and what shows each?
qa.a: Grief, crying in the car park over the trip; frustration, wanting to throw out the machine; and pride in learning the routine and still handing in work.

qa.q: Which moment in the story helped Alka most, and why?
qa.a: The nurse saying all three feelings were allowed, because it stopped Alka feeling like a failure at feelings too.

qa.q: How might Alka's mother have meant "stay positive"?
qa.a: Alka's mother probably meant it lovingly, hoping to protect Alka, without seeing that it made Alka feel judged for the grief.

grounding: Illustrates a person living with long-term illness feeling grief, frustration and pride on the same day, with all of them treated as valid.
